html:
The big picture

The lecture closes the dynamics block and builds the energy toolkit that replaces force-by-force calculations. (1) A friction recap turns into a design question: how hard must a parallel gripper squeeze to hold an object? Static friction, F_F \le \mu_s F_N, answers it. (2) Gravitation gets its direction: in vector form the force always points from one mass toward the other. Dividing out the test mass gives the gravitational field \vec g, the same everywhere for every body. Setting gravity equal to the centripetal force gives the height of a geostationary satellite. (3) Work W = \vec F\cdot\Delta\vec s uses the scalar product. A force that changes along the way, like a spring force F_s = k\,x, needs the integral and gives \tfrac12 k x^2. (4) Net work goes into motion: kinetic energy E_\text{kin} = \tfrac12 m v^2. Work done against a conservative force (gravity, a spring) is stored as potential energy. With only conservative forces, E_\text{kin} + E_\text{pot} stays constant (conservation of energy). (5) Power is work per time, P = \vec F\cdot\vec v.

10 Torque, Gravitation, Work and Energy already covers the scalar law of gravitation, orbital periods, the work integral, E_\text{pot} = mgH and "energy is preserved". This note builds on those sections and doesn't repeat them.

1 Friction recap: static and sliding friction, and a gripper

Lecture: p. 1 top ("Friction", "Example: Parallel gripper") · Giancoli §5-1

Pasted figures, p. 1: a box sliding with velocity \vec v on a surface, friction F_R against the motion, and a magnified view of the contact showing the two rough surfaces interlocking. Below: a box on a floor with F_N up, mg down, an applied force F_A to the right and F_R to the left.

Sliding friction (board): the frictional force does not depend on the velocity nor on the contact area, but on the normal force and the surface properties. The surfaces touch only at the tips of their microscopic bumps; pressing harder squeezes more bumps into contact, so the friction grows in proportion to F_N. This is the friction law of 9 Free-Body Diagrams and Friction › 2 Friction: sliding and static, where the contact-area misconception is also treated.

Static friction and the friction graph. The lecture's graph shows what friction does when you push a resting box harder and harder:

Board, p. 1: friction force F_{R,x} (vertical axis) against the applied force F_{A,x} (horizontal axis). In the middle, labelled "static friction", a straight line of slope -1 through the origin, up to F_{s,\max} = \mu_s\cdot F_N. Beyond it, labelled "dynamic" on both sides, a lower constant level F = \mu_d\cdot F_N.

Read it from the origin outward. While the box rests, friction exactly cancels the push, F_{R,x} = -F_{A,x}, whatever the push is: the slope -1 line. Static friction is a reaction: it is only as large as needed, up to its maximum \mu_s F_N. Once the push exceeds \mu_s F_N the box breaks loose, and friction drops to the sliding value \mu_d F_N, which no longer depends on the push. Because \mu_d < \mu_s, the graph has a step down at the break-away point. The picture is mirror-symmetric: pushing to the left gives the same story with signs reversed.

F_F \le \mu_s\,F_N \ \ \text{(static)}, \qquad F_F = \mu_d\,F_N \ \ \text{(sliding)}
Symbols
  • F_F — friction force (N) (on p. 1 also written F_R, German Reibung; F_{R,x} its x component)
  • F_A — applied force (N); F_{A,x} its x component
  • F_N — normal force between the surfaces (N)
  • \mu_s — coefficient of static friction; \mu_d — coefficient of sliding (dynamic) friction; both dimensionless, \mu_d < \mu_s
  • F_{s,\max} = \mu_s F_N — the largest static friction the contact can supply (N)
Common mistake — "static friction is always \mu_s F_N"

\mu_s F_N is a ceiling, not the value. A book resting on a table has zero friction; push it lightly with 2 N and friction is 2 N. Only at the moment of slipping does static friction reach \mu_s F_N. Use F_F = \mu_s F_N only in a "just about to slip" or "minimum force to hold" question, like the gripper below.

Example: parallel gripper

Lecture: p. 1 ("Example: Parallel gripper") · Giancoli §5-1

Board, p. 1: a block held between two gripper fingers (left and right). Each finger presses with a normal force on the block (F_N' from the left, F_N from the right); each contact carries a friction force F_f pointing up (green). The weight F_g points down from the block's centre. Axes: y up, x to the right.

Given \mu_s = 0.5 and m = 1\ \mathrm{kg}. Which gripping force do we need to apply in order to hold the object?

The object hangs between the fingers; only friction can hold it up, since the normal forces are horizontal. "Hold" means it doesn't slip, so it is at rest (a = 0), and the minimum grip is the one where both contacts are just at their static limit.

F_N' = F_N, \qquad F_f = \mu_s\cdot F_N

The first line is the x direction: the two fingers push from opposite sides, and the block doesn't accelerate sideways, so the two normal forces are equal. The second line is the static limit at each contact. Now the y direction (up positive), with one friction force per finger:

\begin{aligned} 2F_f - m\cdot g &= 0 && \text{(Newton's second law in } y\text{, } a_y = 0) \\ F_f &= \frac{m\cdot g}{2} = \mu_s\cdot F_N = \mu_s\cdot F_N' && \text{(each finger carries half the weight)} \\ F_N &= \frac{m\cdot g}{2\mu_s} = \frac{1\ \mathrm{kg}\cdot 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}}{2\cdot 0.5} = 9.81\ \mathrm{kg\,m/s^2} = 9.81\ \mathrm N && \text{(solve for } F_N) \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • F_N, F_N' — normal (gripping) force of the right and left finger on the block (N)
  • F_f — static friction force at one finger, upward (N)
  • m — mass of the block (kg); g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}; F_g = m g — its weight (N)
  • \mu_s — static friction coefficient between finger and block

Each finger must press with at least 9.81\ \mathrm N, as large as the whole weight. With \mu_s = 0.5 the two contacts together give at most 2 \cdot 0.5\,F_N = F_N of friction, so the total grip must equal mg. A grippier pad (larger \mu_s) lowers the needed force; \mu_s = 1 would halve it.

Problem-solving steps — gripping or clamping with friction
  1. Draw the object with every contact: a normal force into the object and a friction force along the surface at each.
  2. Write the balance across the contacts (x): the normal forces are equal and opposite.
  3. Write the balance along the surfaces (y): the friction forces carry the weight, n\,F_f = mg for n contacts.
  4. At the minimum grip, set each F_f = \mu_s F_N and solve: F_N = \dfrac{mg}{n\,\mu_s}.
  5. Check: a larger \mu_s or more contacts must give a smaller grip.
Connection

This is the sizing rule for a robot gripper: the motor must deliver at least mg/(2\mu_s) per finger, plus a safety factor for the arm's accelerations (an upward acceleration a raises the needed friction to m(g + a)).

2 Gravitation in vector form

Lecture: p. 1 ("Gravitation – Direction") · Giancoli §6-2

10 Torque, Gravitation, Work and Energy › 3 Gravitation gives the size of the gravitational force, F_g = G\,\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2} with G = 6.67\cdot10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2\,kg^{-2}} (board). A force is a vector, so the lecture adds its direction.

Board, p. 1: two masses m_1 (upper right) and m_2 (lower left). In green, the position vectors \vec r_{21} and \vec r_{12} along the line joining them; in red, the forces \vec F_{12} (at m_1, pointing toward m_2) and \vec F_{21} (at m_2, pointing toward m_1).

Naming. \vec F_{12} is the force on m_1 (exerted by m_2). \vec r_{21} points from m_2 to m_1; \vec r_{12} is the same arrow reversed. Both have the same length, the distance between the masses:

r_{21} = r_{12} = r = \lvert\vec r_{21}\rvert, \qquad \vec e_{21} = \frac{\vec r_{21}}{r_{21}} = -\vec e_{12}
Symbols
  • \vec r_{21} — vector from m_2 to m_1 (m); \vec r_{12} = -\vec r_{21} — from m_1 to m_2
  • r — distance between the two (point) masses (m)
  • \vec e_{21} — unit vector from m_2 toward m_1; \vec e_{12} — unit vector from m_1 toward m_2 (dimensionless, length 1)

Gravity always attracts: the force on m_1 points from m_1 toward m_2, along \vec e_{12}. The board writes this first with \vec e_{12} and then rewrites it with \vec r_{21}:

\vec F_{12} = G\,\frac{m_1 m_2}{r_{21}^2}\,\vec e_{12} = -G\,\frac{m_1 m_2}{r_{21}^2}\,\frac{\vec r_{21}}{r_{21}} = -G\,\frac{m_1 m_2}{r_{21}^3}\,\vec r_{21}
Symbols
  • \vec F_{12} — gravitational force on m_1 exerted by m_2 (N), pointing toward m_2
  • G = 6.67\cdot10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2\,kg^{-2}} — universal gravitational constant
  • m_1, m_2 — the two masses (kg); r_{21}, \vec r_{21}, \vec e_{12} — as above

The steps: \vec e_{12} = -\vec e_{21} = -\vec r_{21}/r_{21}, and r_{21}^2 \cdot r_{21} = r_{21}^3. The minus sign is the attraction: \vec r_{21} points away from m_2, the force points back toward it. The r^3 in the denominator is not a stronger law: one power of r only cancels the length of \vec r_{21}, so the size is still G m_1 m_2/r^2.

By the reaction principle (8 Newton's Laws and Forces › 5 Axiom 3: the reaction principle) the force on m_2 is the opposite vector, \vec F_{21} = -\vec F_{12}, as the red arrows show.

Unclear (p. 1): a half-erased line

Below \vec F_{12} = G\frac{m_1 m_2}{r_{21}^2}\cdot\vec e_{12} the page shows "\vec r_{21} = $ … $_{12}" with the middle erased, and a short dash. Most likely the start of "\vec r_{21} = -\vec r_{12}", which the next lines use. Not readable as written.

Common mistake — dropping the minus sign, or the index order

With \vec r_{21} pointing from m_2 to m_1, the force on m_1 is -G\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^3}\vec r_{21}. Without the minus sign the formula describes repulsion. Check the sign with a picture: the force on a body always points toward the other body.

Two small doodles below on p. 1 (a circle with an arrow curling around it, and a small circle) are not labelled; they look like a sketch of a body orbiting the Earth and lead into the satellite example.

3 Satellites: the geostationary orbit

Lecture: p. 2 ("Example: Geostationary Satellite") · Giancoli §6-4

A geostationary satellite stays above the same point of the equator: it circles the Earth exactly once while the Earth turns once. TV and communication satellites use this, so that a dish can point at a fixed spot in the sky. The question is how high such an orbit must be.

The satellite moves on a circle, so the net force on it is a centripetal force; gravity is the only force:

Why a satellite doesn't fall down: it does fall, all the time. Without gravity it would fly straight on (upper path); gravity bends its path down, and at the right speed the curve bends exactly as fast as the Earth's surface curves away below it. (Giancoli Fig. 6-12)

Launch speed decides the orbit near the Earth's surface: about 27,000 km/h gives a circle, more gives an ellipse, about 40,000 km/h escapes for good. A geostationary satellite circles much farther out, where the needed speed is lower. (Giancoli Fig. 6-11)

\sum\vec F_i = m\cdot a_c\cdot\vec e_c, \qquad G\,\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2} = m_2\,\frac{v_2^2}{r}, \qquad v_s = \frac{2\pi r}{T_0}

with (board) m_1 = m_s, v_1 = v_s, m_2 = m_e.

Symbols
  • \vec F_i — forces on the satellite (N); here only gravity
  • a_c = v^2/r — centripetal acceleration (m/s²); \vec e_c — unit vector toward the centre of the circle
  • m_s — satellite mass (kg); m_e — Earth mass (kg); v_s — orbital speed (m/s)
  • r — orbit radius measured from the Earth's centre (m)
  • T_0 — orbital period (s): one sidereal day for a geostationary orbit
Unclear (p. 2): which mass is which

The middle equation writes the right side with m_2 and v_2, but the label list beside it says m_1 = m_s, v_1 = v_s, m_2 = m_e, which would put the Earth's mass and speed on the right. The next line (with m_s cancelled on both sides) shows what was meant: the right side is the satellite's mass times its centripetal acceleration, m_s v_s^2/r.

Which day? The board lists two periods: T = 86\,400\ \mathrm s (24 h, the solar day) and T = 86\,164.1\ \mathrm s (the sidereal day, 23 h 56 min 4 s). The satellite must keep pace with the Earth's rotation relative to the distant stars, which is the sidereal day. The solar day is 4 minutes longer because the Earth also moves along its orbit around the Sun, so it must turn a little extra to bring the Sun back to the same place in the sky.

Solving for r. Insert v_s and cancel the satellite mass, as on the board:

\begin{aligned} G\,\frac{m_e}{r^2}\,m_s &= m_s\left(\frac{2\pi r}{T_0}\right)^2\frac1r && \text{(insert } v_s\text{)} \\ G\,\frac{m_e}{r^2} &= \frac{(2\pi)^2\,r^2}{T_0^2}\cdot\frac1r = \frac{(2\pi)^2\,r}{T_0^2} && \text{(cancel } m_s\text{; one } r \text{ cancels)} \\ r^3 &= \frac{G\,m_e\,T_0^2}{(2\pi)^2} && \text{(multiply by } r^2 T_0^2/(2\pi)^2) \\ r &\approx 42\,200\ \mathrm{km}, \qquad r_s = r - r_e \approx 36\,000\ \mathrm{km} \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • r — orbit radius from the Earth's centre (m); r_e — Earth radius (m); r_s — the satellite's height above the surface (m)
  • G, m_e, T_0 — as above

With G = 6.674\cdot10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}, m_e = 5.97\cdot10^{24}\ \mathrm{kg} and T_0 = 86\,164.1\ \mathrm s: r^3 = 7.49\cdot10^{22}\ \mathrm{m^3}, r = 4.216\cdot10^{7}\ \mathrm m \approx 42\,160\ \mathrm{km}, and with r_e = 6371\ \mathrm{km} the height is r_s \approx 35\,790\ \mathrm{km}. The board's rounded values, "\approx 42\,300 km" and "\approx 36\,000 km", agree within 0.5 %. (With 86 400 s, r is about 80 km larger.) Units: \mathrm{N\,m^2\,kg^{-2}}\cdot\mathrm{kg}\cdot\mathrm{s^2} = \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}\,\mathrm{m^2\,kg^{-1}}\,\mathrm{s^2} = \mathrm{m^3} ✓. The orbital speed is v_s = 2\pi r/T_0 \approx 3.07\ \mathrm{km/s}.

Unclear (p. 2): T_0 without the square

The board writes r^3 = G\,m_e\,\frac{1}{(2\pi)^2}\cdot T_0. The line above it has T_0^2, and the units only give \mathrm m^3 with T_0^2. The square was lost when copying; with T_0 alone the result would be about 955 km, not the 42 300 km written next to it. The board's number belongs to the correct formula with T_0^2.

This is the same route as the orbital period in 10 Torque, Gravitation, Work and Energy › 3 Gravitation (T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^3/(GM)}), run backwards: there r was known and T wanted, here T is fixed and r wanted.

Worked example — a "Mars-stationary" orbit

Mars (M = 6.42\cdot10^{23}\ \mathrm{kg}, radius 3390\ \mathrm{km}) turns once in T_0 = 88\,640\ \mathrm s. How high is a stationary orbit there?

  1. Radius from the planet's centre: r = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{G M T_0^2}{(2\pi)^2}} = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{6.674\cdot10^{-11}\cdot 6.42\cdot10^{23}\cdot 88\,640^2}{4\pi^2}}\ \mathrm m \approx 2.04\cdot10^{7}\ \mathrm m.
  2. Height above the surface: r - r_\text{Mars} \approx 20\,400 - 3390 \approx 17\,000\ \mathrm{km}.
  3. Check: Mars is about ten times lighter than the Earth with almost the same day, and r \propto M^{1/3}: 42\,160\cdot(0.1075)^{1/3}\cdot(88\,640/86\,164)^{2/3} \approx 20\,400\ \mathrm{km} ✓.
Problem-solving steps — orbit for a required period
  1. Fix the period: a stationary orbit uses the planet's rotation period (sidereal day), in seconds.
  2. Set gravity equal to the centripetal force, with v = 2\pi r/T_0; the satellite's mass cancels.
  3. Solve r^3 = G M T_0^2/(2\pi)^2; take the cube root.
  4. Height above ground: subtract the planet's radius. Check that r^3 came out in \mathrm m^3.

4 The gravitational field

Lecture: p. 2 top ("Gravitational Field") · Giancoli §6-8

Gravity acts at a distance, without contact. The field idea describes this: every mass fills the space around it with a gravitational field, and another mass placed there feels a force from the field at its own location. To measure the field at a point, put a small test mass (probe) m_p there and divide the force on it by m_p:

\vec g = \frac{\vec F_p}{m_p}, \qquad \vec F_p = \vec g\cdot m_p
Symbols
  • \vec g — gravitational field at the point (N/kg = m/s²): the gravitational force per kilogram there
  • \vec F_p — gravitational force on the probe (test mass) at that point (N)
  • m_p — mass of the probe (kg), small enough not to disturb the masses that create the field

For the field of one (spherical or point) mass m_2 at distance r, the probe's mass cancels:

g = \frac{F_p}{m_p} = G\,\frac{m_2\cdot m_p}{r^2\cdot m_p} = G\,\frac{m_2}{r^2}, \qquad \vec g = G\cdot\frac{m_1}{r^2}\cdot\vec e_r \ \ \text{(board)}
Symbols
  • g — size of the field (m/s²); m_2 (in the vector line written m_1) — the mass that creates the field (kg)
  • r — distance from that mass's centre to the point (m)
  • \vec e_r — unit vector along the line from the mass to the point

The field depends only on the mass that creates it and on the distance, not on the probe. That is why every body falls with the same acceleration: on the Earth's surface the field is g = G m_e/r_e^2 \approx 9.8\ \mathrm{N/kg}, and \mathrm{N/kg} = \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}/kg} = \mathrm{m/s^2}, the same as the free-fall acceleration of 5 Uniformly Accelerated Motion and Free Fall. The weight \vec F_g = m\vec g of 8 Newton's Laws and Forces › 6 Weight and the normal force is the field equation with the body as the probe.

Unclear (p. 2): the direction of \vec g, and m_1 vs m_2

The board writes \vec g = G\cdot\frac{m_1}{r^2}\cdot\vec e_r, with no minus sign, after using m_2 for the same mass one line above. The field points toward the mass that creates it. If \vec e_r points radially outward (the usual meaning), the correct vector form is \vec g = -G\frac{m}{r^2}\vec e_r, matching the minus sign in \vec F_{12} of section 2. If the lecturer meant \vec e_r to point inward, the board is correct as written. Which convention he uses isn't stated.

Intuition

Think of the field as a map that every point of space carries: "a kilogram placed here is pulled this hard, in this direction". A heavier body is pulled harder in proportion to its mass, so dividing by the mass leaves only the map.

5 Work done by a constant force

Lecture: p. 2 bottom – p. 3 top ("Work & Energy", "Example") · Giancoli §7-1, §7-2

The general definition, W = \int_L\vec F\cdot\mathrm d\vec s, is in 10 Torque, Gravitation, Work and Energy › 4 Work and energy. For a constant force along a straight displacement \Delta\vec r every piece of the path contributes the same, and the integral becomes one scalar product:

W = \vec F\cdot\Delta\vec r = F\,\Delta r\cos\alpha \qquad \text{(scalar product)}
Symbols
  • W — work done by the force \vec F on the body (J = N·m)
  • \vec F — the constant force (N); \Delta\vec r — the body's displacement (m)
  • \alpha — angle between the force and the displacement
  • scalar product as in 2 Vectors and Vector Products › 6 Scalar product ("dot product")

Only the force component along the displacement does work. \cos\alpha sorts the forces: along the motion (\alpha = 0, \cos\alpha = +1) the work is positive; against it (\alpha = 180^\circ, \cos\alpha = -1) negative; across it (\alpha = 90^\circ) zero. Work is a scalar: the works of several forces simply add.

Example (board). Pasted figure: a person pulls a crate along the floor with a rope at an angle; a second sketch shows the free-body diagram: \vec F_N up, \vec F_g down, the pulling force \vec F_P up and to the right at \theta = 37^\circ, friction \vec F_F to the left; the displacement \vec x (40 m) to the right. "180°" is written between \vec F_F and \vec x. Given m = 50\ \mathrm{kg}, F_P = 100\ \mathrm N, \mu_d = 0.1, \theta = 37^\circ, x = 40\ \mathrm m. How much work is done on the crate?

Step 1 – the unknown force. Friction needs F_N, and F_N is not mg here, because the rope pulls partly upward. Force in y direction (no vertical acceleration):

F_N - F_g + F_P\sin\theta = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad F_N = F_g - F_P\sin\theta

so F_N = 50 \cdot 9.81 - 100\sin 37^\circ = 490.5 - 60.2 = 430.3\ \mathrm N, and friction F_F = \mu_d F_N = 43.0\ \mathrm N.

Step 2 – the work of each force, then add:

\begin{aligned} W &= W_g + W_N + W_F + W_P \\ &= 0 + 0 + \mu_d\,(m\,g - F_P\sin\theta)\cdot x\cdot\cos(\alpha) + F_P\cos\theta\cdot x\cdot\cos(\alpha') \end{aligned}

with \cos\alpha = -1 (friction points against the motion) and \cos\alpha' = +1 (the horizontal part of the pull, F_P\cos\theta, points along it).

Symbols
  • W_g, W_N, W_F, W_P — work done by gravity, the normal force, friction and the pull (J)
  • F_g = mg — weight (N); F_P — pulling force in the rope (N); \theta — rope angle above the horizontal
  • \mu_d — sliding friction coefficient; x — distance moved (m)
  • \alpha = 180^\circ — angle between friction and displacement; \alpha' = 0^\circ — angle between F_P\cos\theta and displacement

Gravity and the normal force are vertical, the motion horizontal: \cos 90^\circ = 0, no work. With numbers:

W = -43.0\ \mathrm N\cdot 40\ \mathrm m + 100\ \mathrm N\cdot\cos 37^\circ\cdot 40\ \mathrm m = -1721\ \mathrm J + 3195\ \mathrm J \approx 1.47\cdot10^{3}\ \mathrm J
Unclear (p. 3): "= 1234\ \mathrm{Nm}"

The board's result "1234 Nm" doesn't follow from the given numbers. With g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2} the net work is 1473\ \mathrm J (1475\ \mathrm J with g = 9.8). "1234" looks like a placeholder rather than a calculated value. The brace under (mg - F_P\sin\theta) labels it F_N, and a second brace under \mu_d(\ldots) is labelled "F_F" (written like F_f); both are correct.

Board, in green: "Where does this go? ⇒ Motion". The net work isn't lost: it speeds the crate up. Section 7 makes this exact.

Two more pasted figures (no writing on them, p. 3): a man holding a grocery bag while walking horizontally (\vec F_P up, displacement \vec d sideways), and a hiker climbing a slope of height h with a backpack (\vec d along the slope, angle \theta to the vertical). The bag: the carrying force is perpendicular to the motion, so it does no work (treated in 10 Torque, Gravitation, Work and Energy › 4 Work and energy, "holding or carrying something is work"). The hiker: gravity m\vec g and the displacement \vec d enclose the angle 180^\circ - \theta, so W_g = mg\,d\cos(180^\circ - \theta) = -mg\,d\cos\theta = -mgh, because d\cos\theta is the height gained. The work done by gravity depends only on the height h, not on how steep the path is.

Problem-solving steps — work done by constant forces
  1. Draw the free-body diagram and the displacement; choose x along the motion.
  2. Find any unknown force with Newton's laws first (here F_N from the y balance, then friction).
  3. For each force: W = F\,\Delta r\cos\alpha, with \alpha the angle between that force and the displacement. Forces perpendicular to the motion do no work.
  4. Net work: add the works with their signs (or use the net force: W_\text{net} = F_\text{net}\,\Delta r\cos\alpha).
  5. Check units (J) and that friction's work came out negative.
Common mistake — F_N = mg when a force pulls at an angle

Pulling upward at \theta lifts part of the weight off the floor, so F_N = mg - F_P\sin\theta is smaller than mg, and so is friction. Pushing downward at an angle does the opposite. Get F_N from the vertical balance every time.

6 Work done by a varying force: the spring

Lecture: p. 3 ("Work performed on a spring") · Giancoli §7-3

When the force changes along the path, F\cdot\Delta s no longer works: the work must be added up piece by piece, W = \int\vec F\cdot\mathrm d\vec s. The spring is the standard example.

Pasted figure: (a) a spring fixed to a wall, free end at x = 0; (b) a hand pulls the end out to x > 0 with force \vec F_P (marked "I"); (c) a hand pushes it in to x < 0 (marked "II").

The pasted figure itself. The spring force \vec F_S always points back towards x = 0: to the left when stretched, to the right when compressed. The hand's force \vec F_P is equal and opposite. (Giancoli Fig. 7-10)

To hold a spring stretched (or compressed) by x, you need a force proportional to x:

F_s = k\cdot x, \qquad [k] = \frac{\mathrm N}{\mathrm m}
Symbols
  • F_s — size of the force needed to hold the spring at x (N); the spring itself pulls back with the same size, -k x, toward x = 0
  • k — spring constant (N/m): how many newtons per metre of stretch; a stiff spring has a large k
  • x — stretch from the relaxed length (m): x > 0 stretched, x < 0 compressed

This is Hooke's law; it holds as long as the spring isn't overstretched. The board writes the size k\,x. As a vector, the spring's own force is -k\,x (a restoring force, always back toward x = 0); the person's force is +k\,x.

I: person pulls from 0 to x. The person's force k s points along the stretch at every intermediate stretch s:

W = \int_0^x \vec F\cdot\mathrm d\vec s = \int_0^x k\,s\,\mathrm ds = \tfrac12 k\,s^2\Big|_0^x = \tfrac12 k\,x^2

II: person pushes from 0 to -x. The spring's force at s is -k s; the person pushes against it, -(-k s):

W = -\int_0^{-x}(-k\,s)\,\mathrm ds = \tfrac12 k\,s^2\Big|_0^{-x} = \tfrac12 k\,x^2
Symbols
  • s — the running stretch during the process, from 0 to the final value (m); integration variable
  • W — work done by the person on the spring (J)
  • k, x — as above

In case II both the force and the displacement point in the negative direction, so their product is positive again: compressing costs the same work as stretching by the same amount. The result is the area under the straight force line F = k s, a triangle with base x and height k x: \frac12 \cdot x \cdot kx. A varying force means you can't use "force times distance" with either the start or the end force; for a linear force the average force \frac12 kx gives the right answer.

Why does the integral add up the work correctly?

Cut the stretch into tiny steps \mathrm ds. Over one step the force hardly changes, so that step costs F(s)\,\mathrm ds, the area of a thin strip under the force curve. Adding all strips is the integral, the total area under F(s) from start to end. For a constant force the area is a rectangle, F\cdot\Delta s; for the spring it's a triangle.

Work = area under the force–distance graph. For a spring, F = kx is a straight line, so the area is a triangle: \tfrac12 \cdot x \cdot kx = \tfrac12 k x^2. (Giancoli Fig. 7-11)

Worked example — stretching further costs more

A spring with k = 400\ \mathrm{N/m}. Work to stretch it (a) from 0 to 5 cm, (b) from 5 cm to 10 cm?

  1. (a) W = \tfrac12 k x^2 = \tfrac12\cdot 400\cdot 0.05^2 = 0.5\ \mathrm J.
  2. (b) integral from 0.05 to 0.10: W = \tfrac12 k\,(0.10^2 - 0.05^2) = 200\cdot 0.0075 = 1.5\ \mathrm J.
  3. Point: the second 5 cm cost three times as much as the first, because the spring already pulls back harder. W is not \tfrac12 k(\Delta x)^2 for a stretch that doesn't start at 0.

7 Kinetic energy and the work–energy principle

Lecture: p. 4 ("Kinetic Energy") · Giancoli §7-4

The crate example asked where the net work goes: into motion. The lecture shows this for the simplest case, uniform acceleration from rest by a constant net force F over the distance x:

\vec a = \frac{\sum\vec F_i}{m}, \qquad v = \sqrt{2\,a\,x}, \qquad W = F\cdot x \;\Rightarrow\; x = \frac{W}{F}
v = \sqrt{2\,\frac{F}{m}\cdot\frac{W}{F}} = \sqrt{\frac{2W}{m}} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\,W = \tfrac12\,m\,v^2 = E_\text{kin}\,}
Symbols
  • \sum\vec F_i — net force on the body (N), here constant; F its size along the motion
  • a — the resulting constant acceleration (m/s²); x — distance covered from rest (m)
  • v — speed reached (m/s)
  • W — net work done on the body (J)
  • E_\text{kin} — kinetic energy of the body (J): the energy it has because it moves

The steps: v = \sqrt{2ax} is the time-free law of 5 Uniformly Accelerated Motion and Free Fall (v^2 = v_0^2 + 2ax with v_0 = 0); insert a = F/m (Newton's second law) and x = W/F; F cancels; square both sides and solve for W. The work put in has become the quantity \frac12 m v^2, the kinetic energy.

Starting from a speed v_1 instead of rest, the same steps with v_2^2 = v_1^2 + 2ax give the work–energy principle:

W_\text{net} = \tfrac12 m v_2^2 - \tfrac12 m v_1^2 = \Delta E_\text{kin}
Symbols
  • W_\text{net} — work done by the net force (all forces together) (J)
  • v_1, v_2 — speed before and after (m/s); \Delta E_\text{kin} — change in kinetic energy (J)

Positive net work speeds the body up, negative net work (braking, friction) slows it down. It holds for any force, also a varying one; the constant force just makes the derivation short.

Worked example — the crate's speed after 40 m

The crate of section 5 starts from rest. How fast is it after 40 m?

  1. Net work (section 5): W_\text{net} = 1473\ \mathrm J.
  2. Work–energy principle from rest: \tfrac12 m v^2 = W_\text{net}, so v = \sqrt{2W_\text{net}/m} = \sqrt{2\cdot1473/50} = 7.68\ \mathrm{m/s}.
  3. Check with forces: a = (F_P\cos\theta - F_F)/m = (79.9 - 43.0)/50 = 0.737\ \mathrm{m/s^2}, v = \sqrt{2\cdot0.737\cdot40} = 7.68\ \mathrm{m/s} ✓.
Common mistake — using the work of one force in the work–energy principle

\Delta E_\text{kin} equals the net work, the sum over all forces. In the crate example, the pull alone does 3195 J, but the crate gains only 1473 J of kinetic energy: friction takes 1721 J (as heat). Using W_P alone gives v = 11.3\ \mathrm{m/s}, which is too fast.

8 Potential energy

Lecture: p. 3 bottom ("Potential Energy") – p. 4 top ("Potential Energy of a spring") · Giancoli §8-1, §8-2

10 Torque, Gravitation, Work and Energy › 4 Work and energy introduced E_\text{pot} = mgH as the work stored by lifting. The lecture now states the general rule behind it.

Work against the gravitational field. Lifting a body by h slowly costs W = m\cdot g\cdot h = E_\text{pot}. While it rises, gravity does the opposite work W_g = -mgh on it. The lecture defines the change in potential energy through the work of gravity:

Lifting a brick slowly from y_1 to y_2: the hand's force \vec F_\text{ext} just balances the weight m\vec g and acts over the displacement \vec d of length h = y_2 - y_1, so it does the work mgh. That work is stored as potential energy. (Giancoli Fig. 8-4)

\Delta E_\text{pot} = -W_g = -\int_{P_1}^{P_2} F_g\,\mathrm ds
Symbols
  • \Delta E_\text{pot} = E_\text{pot}(P_2) - E_\text{pot}(P_1) — change in potential energy between points P_1 and P_2 (J)
  • W_g — work done by gravity on the body along the way (J)
  • F_g — gravitational force, \mathrm ds — piece of the path; the integrand is the dot product \vec F_g\cdot\mathrm d\vec s (written without arrows on the board)

Lifting: gravity points down, the motion up, W_g < 0, so E_\text{pot} rises. Falling: W_g > 0, E_\text{pot} falls. The minus sign says that the potential energy is the work gravity can still give back.

This only makes sense because gravity is a conservative force: the work it does between two points depends only on the points, not on the path between them. The hiker of section 5 showed it: steep or gentle, W_g = -mgh. Only a conservative force has a potential energy; for friction the work depends on the path length (a longer detour produces more heat), so there is no "friction potential energy".

Potential energy of a spring. The spring force is conservative too; its potential energy is the work stored by stretching it (section 6), counted from the relaxed spring:

\Delta E = E(x) - E(0) = \tfrac12 k\,x^2
Symbols
  • E(x) — potential energy of the spring at stretch x (J); E(0) = 0 for the relaxed spring
  • k — spring constant (N/m); x — stretch or compression (m)
Intuition

Potential energy is "work on loan". You do work against a conservative force (lifting, stretching); the force can do exactly that work back when you let go. Only the change is defined, so the zero level is a free choice: the floor, the table or the relaxed spring, whichever makes the numbers simplest.

Common mistake — "the potential energy belongs to the object"

A lifted stone has potential energy only together with the Earth that pulls it; a stretched spring stores it in its own deformation. Practically: there is no absolute value of E_\text{pot}, only differences, and a problem must fix one zero level and stick to it.

9 Conservation of energy

Lecture: p. 4 bottom – p. 5 top ("Conservation of Energy") · Giancoli §8-3

Conservation of energy (board): the total energy in a closed system remains constant. For example, if only kinetic and potential energy are involved:

A dropped rock: at the top all potential energy, half-way down half potential and half kinetic, at the bottom all kinetic. The blue bars show U shrinking while the total stays the same. (Giancoli Fig. 8-7)

E_\text{kin} + E_\text{pot} = \text{constant} \qquad \text{(if only conservative forces are acting)}
\frac{\mathrm dE_\text{kin}}{\mathrm dt} = -\frac{\mathrm dE_\text{pot}}{\mathrm dt}, \qquad \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(E_\text{kin} + E_\text{pot}\right) = 0
Symbols
  • E_\text{kin} = \tfrac12 m v^2 — kinetic energy (J); E_\text{pot} — potential energy (J), from gravity (mgh) and/or springs (\tfrac12 kx^2)
  • E_\text{kin} + E_\text{pot} — the mechanical energy of the system
  • \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt} — rate of change per second (J/s)

Where it comes from. If only conservative forces do work, the work–energy principle gives W = \Delta E_\text{kin}, and the definition of potential energy gives W = -\Delta E_\text{pot}. Together:

\Delta E_\text{kin} = -\Delta E_\text{pot} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \Delta\left(E_\text{kin} + E_\text{pot}\right) = 0

Whatever kinetic energy is gained is lost as potential energy, at every moment; that is what the derivative form says. The sum, the mechanical energy, never changes. A falling stone trades height for speed; a swinging pendulum trades back and forth.

The condition matters. Friction is not conservative: with friction, mechanical energy decreases and becomes heat. The total energy, heat included, is still conserved ("no energy is lost", 10 Torque, Gravitation, Work and Energy › 4 Work and energy), but E_\text{kin} + E_\text{pot} alone is not. The next lecture applies both cases (12 Energy Conservation in Practice, Momentum and Collisions).

Worked example — speed from a height, without forces or time

A ball is dropped from h = 5\ \mathrm m. How fast is it 1 m above the ground?

  1. Zero level: the ground. Start: E_\text{kin} = 0, E_\text{pot} = mg\cdot5. At 1 m: E_\text{pot} = mg\cdot1.
  2. Conservation: \tfrac12 m v^2 = mg\,(5 - 1), the mass cancels: v = \sqrt{2g\cdot4} = 8.86\ \mathrm{m/s}.
  3. Check with kinematics: falling 4 m from rest, v^2 = 2g\cdot4 ✓ (5 Uniformly Accelerated Motion and Free Fall).
Problem-solving steps — conservation of mechanical energy
  1. Choose the system and two points: where you know everything (1) and where you want something (2).
  2. Choose the zero level of E_\text{pot} (and the relaxed length for springs).
  3. Check: only conservative forces do work (no friction, no drag)? Then E_\text{kin,1} + E_\text{pot,1} = E_\text{kin,2} + E_\text{pot,2}.
  4. Insert \tfrac12 m v^2, mgh, \tfrac12 k x^2 and solve; often the mass cancels.
  5. Check units and a limiting case (e.g. no height difference → same speed).

10 Power

Lecture: p. 4 ("Power") · Giancoli §8-8

Power is work performed per time. Average and instantaneous power:

\bar P = \frac{W}{\Delta t}, \qquad P = \frac{\mathrm dW}{\mathrm dt} = \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(\vec F\cdot\mathrm d\vec s\right) = \vec F\cdot\frac{\mathrm d\vec s}{\mathrm dt} = \vec F\cdot\vec v
[P] = \frac{\mathrm J}{\mathrm s} = \mathrm W = \mathrm{kg\,m^2/s^3} = \mathrm{N\,m/s}
Symbols
  • \bar P — average power over the time \Delta t (W); P — instantaneous power (W)
  • W — work done in that time (J) (don't confuse with the unit W, watt)
  • \vec F — the force doing the work (N); \vec v — velocity of the point where it acts (m/s); \cdot — scalar product

The middle step is shorthand: the work done in a short time \mathrm dt is \mathrm dW = \vec F\cdot\mathrm d\vec s; dividing by \mathrm dt turns \mathrm d\vec s/\mathrm dt into the velocity. The board marks "scalar product" under \vec F\cdot\vec v: only the force component along the motion delivers power. Remark (board): 1\ \mathrm{hp} = 735.5\ \mathrm W. That is the metric horsepower (PS); the British horsepower in Giancoli is 746 W.

Example (board): a person of m_p = 75\ \mathrm{kg} climbs h_s = 4\ \mathrm m of stairs in t_s = 4\ \mathrm s.

\bar P = \frac{W_s}{t_s} = \frac{m\cdot g\cdot\Delta h}{t_s} = \frac{75\ \mathrm{kg}\cdot 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\cdot 4\ \mathrm m}{4\ \mathrm s} \approx 750\ \mathrm W, \qquad E = \bar P\cdot t_s \approx 3000\ \mathrm J
Symbols
  • W_s — work done lifting the body up the stairs (J); \Delta h = h_s — height climbed (m); t_s — time taken (s)
  • E — energy used for the climb (J)

Exactly: \bar P = 735.75\ \mathrm W, which is 1.0 hp (this is why the remark is there), and E = 2943\ \mathrm J; the board rounds both. Only the lifting counts: the horizontal steps cost no work against gravity. A human can deliver this only for a few seconds.

Intuition

Work says how much; power says how fast. Walking or running up the same stairs takes the same work mgh, but running takes four times less time and so four times the power. A motor is sized by its power: it decides how fast a robot arm can lift a load, while the energy decides how long the battery lasts.

Worked example — power needed to pull at constant speed

A robot drags a 30 kg box across a floor (\mu_d = 0.4) at a constant 0.5\ \mathrm{m/s}, pulling horizontally.

  1. Force: constant speed, so the pull equals friction: F = \mu_d m g = 0.4\cdot30\cdot9.81 = 118\ \mathrm N.
  2. Power: force along the velocity, P = F v = 118\cdot0.5 = 59\ \mathrm W.
  3. Check: in 10 s it moves 5 m, work 118\cdot5 = 589\ \mathrm J, 589/10 = 59\ \mathrm W ✓.
